## Purpose

Closes #54981.

Sentence Transformers can serialize CrossEncoders as explicit module stacks, but vLLM does not currently reconstruct the Transformer → Pooling → Dense layout. The saved pooling behavior and trained Dense scoring head therefore require custom code or manual configuration.

This PR adds bounded support for that exact layout:

- maps cls, mean, and lasttoken pooling to vLLM
- loads the saved Dense weights, bias, and activation
- supports structured text and multimodal query-document messages using the saved chat template
- uses the explicit multimodal text configuration when selecting bidirectional attention
- rejects unsupported pooled configurations rather than silently changing their semantics
- leaves existing non-pooled sequence-classification and CausalLM plus LogitScore paths unchanged

## Test plan

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  tests/entrypoints/pooling/scoring/test_sentence_transformers_io_processor.py \
  tests/models/test_adapters.py \
  tests/transformers_utils/test_config.py \
  tests/transformers_utils/test_repo_utils.py \
  tests/models/transformers/test_backend.py::test_attention_class_selection \
  -k 'cross_encoder or dense_loader or sequence_classification or sentence_transformers or attention_class_selection'
```

## Test result

- 34 passed, 29 deselected
- local pre-commit hooks passed, including Ruff, mypy, SPDX, and configuration validation
- loaded a custom-code-free Mistral 3 VL checkpoint derived from nvidia/rc1-nemotron-3.5-embed with trust_remote_code=False
- scored text, image, and image-plus-text pairs in Sentence Transformers and vLLM; maximum absolute difference was 0.0122

From the Sentence Transformers side, I’m supportive of this approach. Transformer -> Pooling -> Dense is a valid and very reasonable CrossEncoder layout that gives a lot of flexibility with e.g. multimodality in ST. Overall, I'm a big fan of the ST data being parsed and loaded directly, so both vLLM and ST work from the same checkpoint. I also think it's smart to read `modules.json` like you're doing and explicitly reject unsupported ST module configurations (i.e. that don't map to anything meaningful in vLLM at this time). It's also smart to check the `transformer_config` to make sure its a `feature-extraction` ('base model') variant.

I believe the other common variant, just a Transformer except it's a `sequence-classification` variant, is also still supported via the `config.json` where it recognizes the `transformers` classification head.

And then another common format, Transformer -> LogitScore (with the Transformer as a `text-generation` or `any-to-any` variant) is explicitly not implemented here yet, which is okay. That setup 'generates' the logits for the next token, and then either grabs the logits of a specific token ID (e.g. for "yes" or "1") or subtracts the logits of 2 specific token IDs (e.g. "yes" - "no" or "1" - "0") to produce a score.

Lastly, the reported multimodal parity check would probably work well as an integration test. The tests that save a model with Sentence Transformers, load it in vLLM, and compare the scores are a good setup in my opinion.

cc @hmellor as I know you've been interested in easier embedding model deployment as well. Sentence Transformers is really just transformers with some extra small layers on top (dense, pooling, normalize, etc.). It's pretty accessible for vLLM I think.

In Transformers `config.is_causal` is extremely rare, only existing in 4 configs (3 of which are Gemma 4 variants).

Is this a standard field in configs coming from Sentence Transformers?

This is a relatively common "magic field" added in Transformers v5.2.0: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/43705
In short, decorators in `transformers` will pass the config `is_causal` to the attention module and mask creation. It turns the mask bidirectional, as you might've expected. Embedding models and rerankers get a pretty consistent 1-2% improvement with bidirectional attention at a low cost (after all, you can't reuse KV caches with embeddings/rerankers anyways), so I think the majority of new embedding/reranker models are bidirectional (probably still 30-40% of new models just stick with the original causal backbone though).

@@ -118,6 +118,65 @@ The three supported scoring functions are as illustrated in the figure below.
 
 --8<-- [end:supported-cross-encoder-models]
 
+#### Sentence Transformers module checkpoints
+
+vLLM also loads CrossEncoders saved by Sentence Transformers as
+`Transformer → Pooling → Dense` or `Transformer → LogitScore`, without a
+model-specific classification class or `trust_remote_code`. The backbone must be
+supported by vLLM, and the Transformer module must be at the checkpoint root.
+
+```python
+from vllm import LLM
+
+model = LLM("path/to/checkpoint", trust_remote_code=False)
+outputs = model.score("query", ["document one", "document two"])
+```
+
+The checkpoint selects the pooling runner and classification conversion
+automatically. Pooling/Dense exports have a feature-extraction Transformer,
+one `cls`, `mean`, or `lasttoken` pooling mode with
+`include_prompt=True`, and a Dense module mapping `sentence_embedding` to `scores`.
+vLLM loads the trained Dense weights, bias, and activation. CLS pooling requires
+right padding.
+
+LogitScore exports use a `text-generation` or `any-to-any` Transformer producing
+`causal_logits`. vLLM derives a last-token classifier from the saved vocabulary
+IDs: the positive logit alone, or the positive minus negative logit, followed by
+the saved CrossEncoder activation. This requires unquantized merged weights,
+TP=PP=1, and a bias-free linear LM head without logit scaling or soft-capping;
+runtime LoRA adapters are not supported.
+
+LogitScore message inputs support saved default and named system prompts, plus
+boolean `add_generation_prompt` and `enable_thinking` settings under
+`processing_kwargs.chat_template`. Request chat-template kwargs override saved
+settings: `prompt` overrides `prompt_name`, and `prompt=""` disables the default.
+For example, select a saved prompt with
+`PoolingParams(extra_kwargs={"chat_template_kwargs": {"prompt_name": "match"}})`.
+
+Ordinary text pairs use tokenizer pair encoding. Exports declaring `flat` or
+`structured` message inputs use their saved chat template with `query` and
+`document` roles. Flat inputs accept strings or a single text content part;
+multimodal pairs require structured messages and a compatible backbone. Text and
+image pairs are tested; arbitrary any-to-any models, audio, and video are not.
+The saved tokenizer length limit is used by default. Explicit tokenization options
+can override automatic truncation.
+
+Modular CrossEncoders with token type embeddings, such as BERT, require a native
+vLLM implementation. BERT uses this by default; selecting
+`model_impl="transformers"` is rejected for these checkpoints. Existing non-modular
+embedding and sequence-classification checkpoints are unaffected.
+
+Unsupported topologies and processing settings are rejected instead of silently
+changing checkpoint behavior. Pooling/Dense additionally rejects saved prompts,
+residual Dense layers, and prompt-excluding pooling. Existing model-specific
+reranker paths are unchanged.
+
+Saved CrossEncoder output activations take precedence over the backbone's
+`problem_type`, including the legacy `sbert_ce_default_activation_function`
+setting. A saved Sigmoid remains a sigmoid even for multi-output classifiers.
+Use `PoolingParams(use_activation=False)` to skip the final CrossEncoder
+activation; any activation within the Dense module still applies.
+
 ### Late-interaction models
 
 All models that support token embedding task also support using the score API to compute similarity scores by calculating the late interaction of two input prompts. See [this page](token_embed.md) for more information about token embedding models.

This is a relatively common "magic field" added in Transformers v5.2.0: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/43705
In short, decorators in `transformers` will pass the config `is_causal` to the attention module and mask creation. It turns the mask bidirectional, as you might've expected. Embedding models and rerankers get a pretty consistent 1-2% improvement with bidirectional attention at a low cost (after all, you can't reuse KV caches with embeddings/rerankers anyways), so I think the majority of new embedding/reranker models are bidirectional (probably still 30-40% of new models just stick with the original causal backbone though).

From the Sentence Transformers side, I’m supportive of this approach. Transformer -> Pooling -> Dense is a valid and very reasonable CrossEncoder layout that gives a lot of flexibility with e.g. multimodality in ST. Overall, I'm a big fan of the ST data being parsed and loaded directly, so both vLLM and ST work from the same checkpoint. I also think it's smart to read `modules.json` like you're doing and explicitly reject unsupported ST module configurations (i.e. that don't map to anything meaningful in vLLM at this time). It's also smart to check the `transformer_config` to make sure its a `feature-extraction` ('base model') variant.

I believe the other common variant, just a Transformer except it's a `sequence-classification` variant, is also still supported via the `config.json` where it recognizes the `transformers` classification head.

And then another common format, Transformer -> LogitScore (with the Transformer as a `text-generation` or `any-to-any` variant) is explicitly not implemented here yet, which is okay. That setup 'generates' the logits for the next token, and then either grabs the logits of a specific token ID (e.g. for "yes" or "1") or subtracts the logits of 2 specific token IDs (e.g. "yes" - "no" or "1" - "0") to produce a score.

Lastly, the reported multimodal parity check would probably work well as an integration test. The tests that save a model with Sentence Transformers, load it in vLLM, and compare the scores are a good setup in my opinion.

cc @hmellor as I know you've been interested in easier embedding model deployment as well. Sentence Transformers is really just transformers with some extra small layers on top (dense, pooling, normalize, etc.). It's pretty accessible for vLLM I think.
